Proposition 43 Supporters and Opponents
What Would Proposition 43 Do?
This measure would require at least two-thirds of local voters to approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax. The measure would apply to initiatives placed on a local ballot on or after January 1, 2027.
This new supermajority vote requirement would apply to special tax voter initiatives raising revenue for many types of local governments, including cities, counties, special districts, and other local or regional government entity. 1 (javascript:void(0)) Under California’s Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C), all taxes levied by special districts are considered “special taxes,” so Prop. 43’s two-thirds vote requirement would apply to any taxes placed on the ballot by voters to generate revenues for special districts as well as city and county taxes for dedicated purposes.
Glossary of Key Terms
General tax
Local voter initiative process
Parcel tax
Simple majority vote
Special tax
Supermajority vote
General tax
A tax that is levied by a city or county and that may be spent on any program or service. All non-property taxes that cities and counties may levy can be imposed as general taxes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) . A general tax may be approved by a simple majority of local voters, regardless of whether it is placed on the ballot by the local government entity or by a local voter initiative.
Local voter initiative process
Gives residents of a city or a county the power to propose changes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2011.&article=II) to local ordinances. This process involves a number of steps, including drafting a ballot measure, circulating petitions, and gathering the required signatures.
Parcel tax
A tax on a parcel of property that is not based on the property value. This tax is generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square-foot or per-room basis. Parcel taxes can be levied by cities, counties, school districts, community college districts, and most special districts. Parcel taxes are always considered to be special taxes for the purpose of determining voter-approval requirements.
Simple majority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive support from at least half of voters plus one additional voter (50%+1) in order to be approved.
Special tax
Includes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) 1) parcel taxes, 2) city or county taxes (excluding property taxes) dedicated to specific purposes, and 3) taxes (excluding property taxes) levied by special purpose districts — that is, special districts, K-12 school districts, and community college districts.
Supermajority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive more than a simple majority vote, such as three-fifths or two-thirds, in order to be approved.
What Are the Current Vote Requirements for Local Revenue Increases in California?
California’s Constitution has a complex set of rules governing how local governments can raise taxes and other types of revenue. These rules were put in place by statewide ballot measures over the past several decades (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx#Voter_Approval_Requirements_For_Taxes:~:text=Major%20Milestones%20in%20the%20Development%20of%20Voter%E2%80%93Approval%20Requirements%20for%20Local%20Taxes), beginning with Prop. 13 in 1978 and followed by other measures creating additional restrictions on local revenue-raising capacity, including Prop. 62 (1986) and Prop. 218 (1996).
These rules apply to local measures to create new taxes as well as to increase or extend any existing tax.
Tax measures proposed by local governments — such as city councils or county boards of supervisors — must go on the ballot and be approved by voters. Current voter-approval thresholds differ depending on the type of tax that would be raised:
A general tax requires only a simple majority vote to pass, with the revenue available for any program or service.
A special tax requires a two-thirds vote to pass, and includes a tax dedicated to a specific purpose.
Special taxes proposed through the local voter initiative process are subject to different rules. In recent years, a series of court decisions (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2021/a157983.html) have clarified that the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes in the state Constitution does not apply to special tax measures placed on the ballot by local voter initiative. Therefore, both general taxes and special taxes proposed by voters can be approved with a simple majority vote . 2 (javascript:void(0)) Several cases involving special tax voter initiatives that were approved with a simple majority vote were appealed to the California Supreme Court, but the Supreme Court denied review of the appellate court decisions, allowing these decisions to stand. A variety of special tax initiatives have been approved over the past several years with a simple majority vote, such as:
San Francisco’s Measure C in November 2018, creating a tax on commercial landlords to raise funds for child care and early education, which passed with 51% of the vote.
Fresno’s Measure P in November 2018, increasing the local sales tax rate to fund community parks, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Los Angeles’ Measure ULA in November 2022, creating a property transfer tax on sales of high-value property to raise funds for affordable housing development and homelessness service, which passed with 58% of the vote.
Madera County’s Measure T in November 2024, renewing a local sales tax rate to fund transportation projects, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Certain types of local taxes are always classified as special taxes for the purposes of voter approval requirements. This includes:
Taxes levied by special-purpose districts, including school districts, community college districts, and special districts.
Parcel taxes, which are taxes on parcels of property that are not based on the property value . These taxes are generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square foot or per-room basis.
What Services Do Local Governments in California Provide?
Californians in every community across the state benefit from services provided by local governments. Local services help keep people safe and healthy by providing fire protection, law enforcement, public health services, hospitals and emergency services, road safety, and more. Local governments also provide educational and recreational spaces like public libraries, public parks, and playgrounds.
Californians experiencing economic insecurity, food security, or who don’t have access to private health insurance can access financial assistance, food assistance, and health care because counties are there to administer public health and economic security programs. Cities can support the development of affordable housing to ensure more of their residents can afford a safe place to live.
The services provided by California’s local governments vary according to the type of entity (https://www.ca-ilg.org/sites/main/files/file-attachments/who_does_what.pdf):
Counties administer health and human services programs such as Medi-Cal (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/medi-cal/) health coverage, CalFresh (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calfresh/) food assistance, and CalWORKs (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calworks/) cash assistance for families. Counties also provide public health, behavioral health, and child welfare services. Additionally, counties are responsible (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/california-county-budget-process-guide/) for overseeing the local justice system and courts, administering elections, and providing municipal services like sewer systems and trash pick-up in unincorporated areas.
Cities provide a variety of municipal services such as fire protection, housing and urban planning, parks and recreation, libraries, street repair, water and sewer systems, and law enforcement — although some of these services may be provided by special districts in some areas.
Special districts provide specialized services such as fire protection, water, electricity, parks and recreation, transit, hospitals, and other health care services.
Regional entities such as Joint Powers Authorities and Councils of Government coordinate policy and service provision across regions spanning multiple cities or counties, such as regional transportation authorities.
How Do Local Governments Raise Revenue?
Local governments in California rely on a variety of revenue sources, including transfers from the state and federal governments, allocations of local property taxes, and various other taxes, service charges, assessments, and fees.
Most types of local governments receive some revenues from the local property tax, capped at 1% by Prop. 13 (1978). Property taxes are collected by counties and the revenues are allocated (https://propertytax.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2026/revenue/0/entity_type?vis=pieChart) to support city and county governments, school districts, community college districts, and special districts in accordance with formulas established in state law. Local governments and voters cannot increase property taxes beyond the 1% rate, except to finance infrastructure bonds. 3 (javascript:void(0)) Property tax increases to support school infrastructure bonds can generally be approved by 55% of local voters. All other property taxes for infrastructure bonds must be approved by two-thirds of voters.

Other common types of taxes supporting local services include sales taxes (known as transactions and use taxes at the local level), taxes on hotel stays (known as transient occupancy taxes), property transfer taxes, utility user taxes, and business license taxes.
The revenues that make up local government budgets vary by the type of entity (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx#Voter_Approval_Requirements_For_Taxes:~:text=Local%20Governments%20Levy%20Many%20Types%20of%20Taxes), and the legal authority to raise taxes (https://www.ca-ilg.org/sites/main/files/file-attachments/resources__Revenues_and_Responsibilities.pdf) also differs by government type. Cities and counties have fairly broad authority to raise a variety of taxes — with voter approval — while special districts have more limited authority. These districts are largely limited to parcel taxes — a tax on parcels of land not based on their value — as a source of discretionary revenue, although some can levy district sales taxes and certain other types of taxes.
More than half of county-level revenues (https://counties.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/category?vis=pieChart) statewide come from the state and federal governments and local property taxes. Other types of taxes make up a small share of total county revenues — generally less than 3%. Common types of taxes levied by counties include sales taxes, property transfer taxes, taxes on hotel stays, and utility user taxes.
City-level revenues (https://cities.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/subcategory_1?vis=pieChart) primarily come from service charges for municipal functions — such as electricity, water, and sewer services — and various taxes. These two categories generally each make up around one-third of total city revenues statewide. Local property tax revenues and sales taxes are the largest sources of tax revenues for cities, each representing about one-quarter of tax revenues. Issue Brief
Should California Voters Approve Proposition 43?
What the Supermajority Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives Would Mean for California Communities
August 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would require that at least two-thirds of local voters approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax, starting on January 1, 2027. As communities across California are facing substantial challenges and uncertainties, this measure would make it harder for local voters to raise revenues to support local public services and give outsized power to a small share of voters. Approval of the measure would decrease the likelihood that local governments meet the needs of their residents and could increase hardship in some communities throughout the state.

What Would Proposition 43 Do?
This measure would require at least two-thirds of local voters to approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax. The measure would apply to initiatives placed on a local ballot on or after January 1, 2027.
This new supermajority vote requirement would apply to special tax voter initiatives raising revenue for many types of local governments, including cities, counties, special districts, and other local or regional government entity. 1 (javascript:void(0)) Under California’s Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C), all taxes levied by special districts are considered “special taxes,” so Prop. 43’s two-thirds vote requirement would apply to any taxes placed on the ballot by voters to generate revenues for special districts as well as city and county taxes for dedicated purposes.
Glossary of Key Terms
General tax
Local voter initiative process
Parcel tax
Simple majority vote
Special tax
Supermajority vote
General tax
A tax that is levied by a city or county and that may be spent on any program or service. All non-property taxes that cities and counties may levy can be imposed as general taxes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) . A general tax may be approved by a simple majority of local voters, regardless of whether it is placed on the ballot by the local government entity or by a local voter initiative.
Local voter initiative process
Gives residents of a city or a county the power to propose changes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2011.&article=II) to local ordinances. This process involves a number of steps, including drafting a ballot measure, circulating petitions, and gathering the required signatures.
Parcel tax
A tax on a parcel of property that is not based on the property value. This tax is generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square-foot or per-room basis. Parcel taxes can be levied by cities, counties, school districts, community college districts, and most special districts. Parcel taxes are always considered to be special taxes for the purpose of determining voter-approval requirements.
Simple majority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive support from at least half of voters plus one additional voter (50%+1) in order to be approved.
Special tax
Includes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) 1) parcel taxes, 2) city or county taxes (excluding property taxes) dedicated to specific purposes, and 3) taxes (excluding property taxes) levied by special purpose districts — that is, special districts, K-12 school districts, and community college districts.
Supermajority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive more than a simple majority vote, such as three-fifths or two-thirds, in order to be approved.
What Are the Current Vote Requirements for Local Revenue Increases in California?
California’s Constitution has a complex set of rules governing how local governments can raise taxes and other types of revenue. These rules were put in place by statewide ballot measures over the past several decades (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx#Voter_Approval_Requirements_For_Taxes:~:text=Major%20Milestones%20in%20the%20Development%20of%20Voter%E2%80%93Approval%20Requirements%20for%20Local%20Taxes), beginning with Prop. 13 in 1978 and followed by other measures creating additional restrictions on local revenue-raising capacity, including Prop. 62 (1986) and Prop. 218 (1996).
These rules apply to local measures to create new taxes as well as to increase or extend any existing tax.
Tax measures proposed by local governments — such as city councils or county boards of supervisors — must go on the ballot and be approved by voters. Current voter-approval thresholds differ depending on the type of tax that would be raised:
A general tax requires only a simple majority vote to pass, with the revenue available for any program or service.
A special tax requires a two-thirds vote to pass, and includes a tax dedicated to a specific purpose.
Special taxes proposed through the local voter initiative process are subject to different rules. In recent years, a series of court decisions (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2021/a157983.html) have clarified that the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes in the state Constitution does not apply to special tax measures placed on the ballot by local voter initiative. A variety of special tax initiatives have been approved over the past several years with a simple majority vote, such as:
San Francisco’s Measure C in November 2018, creating a tax on commercial landlords to raise funds for child care and early education, which passed with 51% of the vote.
Fresno’s Measure P in November 2018, increasing the local sales tax rate to fund community parks, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Los Angeles’ Measure ULA in November 2022, creating a property transfer tax on sales of high-value property to raise funds for affordable housing development and homelessness service, which passed with 58% of the vote.
Madera County’s Measure T in November 2024, renewing a local sales tax rate to fund transportation projects, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Certain types of local taxes are always classified as special taxes for the purposes of voter approval requirements. This includes:
Taxes levied by special-purpose districts, including school districts, community college districts, and special districts.
Parcel taxes, which are taxes on parcels of property that are not based on the property value . These taxes are generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square foot or per-room basis.
What Services Do Local Governments in California Provide?
Californians in every community across the state benefit from services provided by local governments. Local services help keep people safe and healthy by providing fire protection, law enforcement, public health services, hospitals and emergency services, road safety, and more. Local governments also provide educational and recreational spaces like public libraries, public parks, and playgrounds.
Californians experiencing economic insecurity, food security, or who don’t have access to private health insurance can access financial assistance, food assistance, and health care because counties are there to administer public health and economic security programs. Cities can support the development of affordable housing to ensure more of their residents can afford a safe place to live.
The services provided by California’s local governments vary according to the type of entity (https://www.ca-ilg.org/sites/main/files/file-attachments/who_does_what.pdf):
Counties administer health and human services programs such as Medi-Cal (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/medi-cal/) health coverage, CalFresh (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calfresh/) food assistance, and CalWORKs (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calworks/) cash assistance for families. Counties also provide public health, behavioral health, and child welfare services. Additionally, counties are responsible (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/california-county-budget-process-guide/) for overseeing the local justice system and courts, administering elections, and providing municipal services like sewer systems and trash pick-up in unincorporated areas.
Cities provide a variety of municipal services such as fire protection, housing and urban planning, parks and recreation, libraries, street repair, water and sewer systems, and law enforcement — although some of these services may be provided by special districts in some areas.
Special districts provide specialized services such as fire protection, water, electricity, parks and recreation, transit, hospitals, and other health care services.
Regional entities such as Joint Powers Authorities and Councils of Government coordinate policy and service provision across regions spanning multiple cities or counties, such as regional transportation authorities.
How Do Local Governments Raise Revenue?
Local governments in California rely on a variety of revenue sources, including transfers from the state and federal governments, allocations of local property taxes, and various other taxes, service charges, assessments, and fees.
Most types of local governments receive some revenues from the local property tax, capped at 1% by Prop. 13 (1978). Property taxes are collected by counties and the revenues are allocated (https://propertytax.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2026/revenue/0/entity_type?vis=pieChart) to support city and county governments, school districts, community college districts, and special districts in accordance with formulas established in state law. Local governments and voters cannot increase property taxes beyond the 1% rate, except to finance infrastructure bonds. 3 (javascript:void(0)) Property tax increases to support school infrastructure bonds can generally be approved by 55% of local voters. All other property taxes for infrastructure bonds must be approved by two-thirds of voters.

- Uniformity: A special tax is a special tax; Prop 13/218's two-thirds requirement should apply regardless of the procedural path. - Also there's an argument that earmarked special taxes reduce budget flexibility; the two-thirds requirement forces broad consensus.

Case for NO:
- Restricts direct democracy; 34% minority veto. Contrary to the principle that the initiative power should be liberally construed and that voters should be able to govern themselves.
- Reduces revenue for essential local services at a time of federal cuts, wildfire recovery, housing crisis. Examples: county fire/paramedic taxes, homeless services, transit, open space.
- Also applies to "extend" — so renewals of expiring citizen-initiated special taxes would need two-thirds, creating fiscal cliffs. Aleshire & Wynder note the greatest impact would be on future proposals to extend/renew existing voter-approved special taxes — meaning existing programs funded at majority-level support may lapse. That's a significant hidden risk: taxes that voters approved years ago with e.g. 60% support would now fail to renew.
- Hidden provision (b) banning citizen-initiated ad valorem property taxes — not in the official title/summary or LAO analysis. Undisclosed scope.
- The Yes campaign's official argument makes claims that are not in the text (spending accountability, "guarantees right to vote on all local taxes," transfer tax protection), i.e., misleading.
- The author of the measure opposes it; Democratic legislators who placed it on the ballot did so under duress and are urging a no vote. The Legislature's near-unanimous vote is being used as evidence of legitimacy, but it was a hostage negotiation.
- Funded overwhelmingly by big business (California Business Roundtable, real estate developers) seeking to limit local revenue options; part of a package (Props 41, 42) aimed at constraining taxation, including the billionaire tax.
- Majority of likely voters oppose.
- Also: Prop 43 doesn't address the actual problem it claims (high cost of living) — it cuts no taxes, per the rebuttal.

Weighing: I think "no" is the better-supported recommendation for a typical California voter: it preserves majority rule and local self-determination, avoids undisclosed restrictions, and avoids revenue losses for fire/EMS/schools/housing during a period of fiscal stress. The consistency/loophole argument has some intellectual force but the practical effect is to entrench minority rule in local taxation and reduce funding for services; plus the measure was sold with arguments not supported by its text.

Also consider: does voting no risk bringing back the worse HJTA initiative? Possibly in 2028, but the deal was already executed — HJTA withdrew it, and they got the compromise on the ballot. If voters reject it, HJTA could re-qualify. But that's speculative and shouldn't drive the vote; also the broader measure faced unified opposition from cities, counties, fire groups, and would likely lose too.

I'll answer "no". Let me do a bit more research to be thorough — check the Budget Center page and remaining cityhallpass content on interactions, plus KQED opponent analysis. Then answer with only "no".

XVIII, Sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)). The new two-thirds rule begins Jan. 1, 2027 (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
What it covers. New, increased or extended special taxes proposed by voters and approved after Jan. 1, 2027 (official summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/title-summary.htm); Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)).
Open questions. Subdivision (b), on taxes based on property value, is not explained in the Legislative Analyst’s analysis (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)). Burke, Williams & Sorensen says it will watch “any subsequent litigation or implementing legislation” (California City News (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)). We found no lawsuit filed against the measure as of Sept. 30, 2026.
Key moments
We found no televised debate on Proposition 43 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
Deal and same-day vote (June 25, 2026). The Jarvis initiative and ACA 13 were pulled and ACA 22 passed both houses the same day (ACA 22 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22); LAist (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure); Burke, Williams & Sorensen (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)).
ULA changes shelved in LA (July 1, 2026). Councilmember Katy Yaroslavsky, who proposed the 10-year apartment exemption, said “If we think the fight is over, we’re kidding ourselves” (LAist (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-council-mansion-tax-measure-ula-november-ballot-measure-2026-vote)).
The author opposes her measure (July 2026). Wicks urged a no vote, as reported by the LA Times and noted by the Orange County Register’s editorial board (LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits); Orange County Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/09/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-43-to-make-it-harder-to-raise-taxes/)).

Issue Brief
Should California Voters Approve Proposition 43?
What the Supermajority Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives Would Mean for California Communities
August 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would require that at least two-thirds of local voters approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax, starting on January 1, 2027. As communities across California are facing substantial challenges and uncertainties, this measure would make it harder for local voters to raise revenues to support local public services and give outsized power to a small share of voters. Approval of the measure would decrease the likelihood that local governments meet the needs of their residents and could increase hardship in some communities throughout the state.
table of contents
What Would Proposition 43 Do?
Glossary of Key Terms
What Are the Current Vote Requirements for Local Revenue Increases in California?
What Services Do Local Governments in California Provide?
How Do Local Governments Raise Revenue?
How Would Proposition 43 Affect California Communities?
Proposition 43 Supporters and Opponents
What Would Proposition 43 Do?
This measure would require at least two-thirds of local voters to approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax. The measure would apply to initiatives placed on a local ballot on or after January 1, 2027.
This new supermajority vote requirement would apply to special tax voter initiatives raising revenue for many types of local governments, including cities, counties, special districts, and other local or regional government entity. 1 (javascript:void(0)) Under California’s Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C), all taxes levied by special districts are considered “special taxes,” so Prop. 43’s two-thirds vote requirement would apply to any taxes placed on the ballot by voters to generate revenues for special districts as well as city and county taxes for dedicated purposes.
Glossary of Key Terms
General tax
Local voter initiative process
Parcel tax
Simple majority vote
Special tax
Supermajority vote
General tax
A tax that is levied by a city or county and that may be spent on any program or service. All non-property taxes that cities and counties may levy can be imposed as general taxes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) . A general tax may be approved by a simple majority of local voters, regardless of whether it is placed on the ballot by the local government entity or by a local voter initiative.
Local voter initiative process
Gives residents of a city or a county the power to propose changes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2011.&article=II) to local ordinances. This process involves a number of steps, including drafting a ballot measure, circulating petitions, and gathering the required signatures.
Parcel tax
A tax on a parcel of property that is not based on the property value. This tax is generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square-foot or per-room basis. Parcel taxes can be levied by cities, counties, school districts, community college districts, and most special districts. Parcel taxes are always considered to be special taxes for the purpose of determining voter-approval requirements.
Simple majority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive support from at least half of voters plus one additional voter (50%+1) in order to be approved.
Special tax
Includes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) 1) parcel taxes, 2) city or county taxes (excluding property taxes) dedicated to specific purposes, and 3) taxes (excluding property taxes) levied by special purpose districts — that is, special districts, K-12 school districts, and community college districts.
Supermajority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive more than a simple majority vote, such as three-fifths or two-thirds, in order to be approved.
What Are the Current Vote Requirements for Local Revenue Increases in California?
California’s Constitution has a complex set of rules governing how local governments can raise taxes and other types of revenue. These rules were put in place by statewide ballot measures over the past several decades (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx#Voter_Approval_Requirements_For_Taxes:~:text=Major%20Milestones%20in%20the%20Development%20of%20Voter%E2%80%93Approval%20Requirements%20for%20Local%20Taxes), beginning with Prop. 13 in 1978 and followed by other measures creating additional restrictions on local revenue-raising capacity, including Prop. 62 (1986) and Prop. 218 (1996).
These rules apply to local measures to create new taxes as well as to increase or extend any existing tax.
Tax measures proposed by local governments — such as city councils or county boards of supervisors — must go on the ballot and be approved by voters. Current voter-approval thresholds differ depending on the type of tax that would be raised:
A general tax requires only a simple majority vote to pass, with the revenue available for any program or service.
A special tax requires a two-thirds vote to pass, and includes a tax dedicated to a specific purpose.
Special taxes proposed through the local voter initiative process are subject to different rules. In recent years, a series of court decisions (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2021/a157983.html) have clarified that the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes in the state Constitution does not apply to special tax measures placed on the ballot by local voter initiative. Therefore, both general taxes and special taxes proposed by voters can be approved with a simple majority vote . 2 (javascript:void(0)) Several cases involving special tax voter initiatives that were approved with a simple majority vote were appealed to the California Supreme Court, but the Supreme Court denied review of the appellate court decisions, allowing these decisions to stand. A variety of special tax initiatives have been approved over the past several years with a simple majority vote, such as:
San Francisco’s Measure C in November 2018, creating a tax on commercial landlords to raise funds for child care and early education, which passed with 51% of the vote.
Fresno’s Measure P in November 2018, increasing the local sales tax rate to fund community parks, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Los Angeles’ Measure ULA in November 2022, creating a property transfer tax on sales of high-value property to raise funds for affordable housing development and homelessness service, which passed with 58% of the vote.
Madera County’s Measure T in November 2024, renewing a local sales tax rate to fund transportation projects, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Certain types of local taxes are always classified as special taxes for the purposes of voter approval requirements. This includes:
Taxes levied by special-purpose districts, including school districts, community college districts, and special districts.
Parcel taxes, which are taxes on parcels of property that are not based on the property value . These taxes are generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square foot or per-room basis.
What Services Do Local Governments in California Provide?
Californians in every community across the state benefit from services provided by local governments. Local services help keep people safe and healthy by providing fire protection, law enforcement, public health services, hospitals and emergency services, road safety, and more. Local governments also provide educational and recreational spaces like public libraries, public parks, and playgrounds.
Californians experiencing economic insecurity, food security, or who don’t have access to private health insurance can access financial assistance, food assistance, and health care because counties are there to administer public health and economic security programs. Cities can support the development of affordable housing to ensure more of their residents can afford a safe place to live.
The services provided by California’s local governments vary according to the type of entity (https://www.ca-ilg.org/sites/main/files/file-attachments/who_does_what.pdf):
Counties administer health and human services programs such as Medi-Cal (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/medi-cal/) health coverage, CalFresh (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calfresh/) food assistance, and CalWORKs (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calworks/) cash assistance for families. Counties also provide public health, behavioral health, and child welfare services. Additionally, counties are responsible (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/california-county-budget-process-guide/) for overseeing the local justice system and courts, administering elections, and providing municipal services like sewer systems and trash pick-up in unincorporated areas.
Cities provide a variety of municipal services such as fire protection, housing and urban planning, parks and recreation, libraries, street repair, water and sewer systems, and law enforcement — although some of these services may be provided by special districts in some areas.
Special districts provide specialized services such as fire protection, water, electricity, parks and recreation, transit, hospitals, and other health care services.
Regional entities such as Joint Powers Authorities and Councils of Government coordinate policy and service provision across regions spanning multiple cities or counties, such as regional transportation authorities.
How Do Local Governments Raise Revenue?
Local governments in California rely on a variety of revenue sources, including transfers from the state and federal governments, allocations of local property taxes, and various other taxes, service charges, assessments, and fees.
Most types of local governments receive some revenues from the local property tax, capped at 1% by Prop. 13 (1978). Property taxes are collected by counties and the revenues are allocated (https://propertytax.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2026/revenue/0/entity_type?vis=pieChart) to support city and county governments, school districts, community college districts, and special districts in accordance with formulas established in state law. Local governments and voters cannot increase property taxes beyond the 1% rate, except to finance infrastructure bonds. 3 (javascript:void(0)) Property tax increases to support school infrastructure bonds can generally be approved by 55% of local voters. All other property taxes for infrastructure bonds must be approved by two-thirds of voters.
Curious About Other Ballot Propositions?
Browse our collection of resources covering California’s statewide ballot measures to help you understand what’s at stake for California this November.
See More Resources (https://calbudgetcenter.org/issues/ballot-propositions/)
Other common types of taxes supporting local services include sales taxes (known as transactions and use taxes at the local level), taxes on hotel stays (known as transient occupancy taxes), property transfer taxes, utility user taxes, and business license taxes.
The revenues that make up local government budgets vary by the type of entity (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx#Voter_Approval_Requirements_For_Taxes:~:text=Local%20Governments%20Levy%20Many%20Types%20of%20Taxes), and the legal authority to raise taxes (https://www.ca-ilg.org/sites/main/files/file-attachments/resources__Revenues_and_Responsibilities.pdf) also differs by government type. Cities and counties have fairly broad authority to raise a variety of taxes — with voter approval — while special districts have more limited authority. These districts are largely limited to parcel taxes — a tax on parcels of land not based on their value — as a source of discretionary revenue, although some can levy district sales taxes and certain other types of taxes.
More than half of county-level revenues (https://counties.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/category?vis=pieChart) statewide come from the state and federal governments and local property taxes. Other types of taxes make up a small share of total county revenues — generally less than 3%. Common types of taxes levied by counties include sales taxes, property transfer taxes, taxes on hotel stays, and utility user taxes.
City-level revenues (https://cities.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/subcategory_1?vis=pieChart) primarily come from service charges for municipal functions — such as electricity, water, and sewer services — and various taxes. These two categories generally each make up around one-third of total city revenues statewide. Local property tax revenues and sales taxes are the largest sources of tax revenues for cities, each representing about one-quarter of tax revenues. Other major tax revenue sources for cities include taxes on hotel stays, utility user taxes, and business license taxes.
Special district revenues (https://districts.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/subcategory_2?vis=pieChart) come largely from customer service charges for the service provided by the district, local property taxes, and certain other taxes and assessments, depending on the type of district. 4 (javascript:void(0)) The composition of special district revenues depends on the type of special district (https://sgf.senate.ca.gov/sites/sgf.senate.ca.gov/files/special_district_facts_2016.pdf). Enterprise districts provide services to customers for a charge and operate similar to businesses, being largely financed by user charges. Examples of enterprise districts include health care districts, airport districts, water districts, and other utility districts. Non-enterprise districts provide benefits to entire communities — such as fire protection and road repair services — and are primarily funded by property taxes and other types of taxes and assessments. As noted above, taxes levied by special districts are always considered special taxes so they require approval of two-thirds of voters in the district, unless they are placed on the ballot by voters.
How Would Proposition 43 Affect California Communities?
Proposition 43 Would Make It More Difficult for Communities to Generate Revenues to Meet Local Needs
California already imposes high barriers to raising local revenues by requiring all special taxes levied by local governments to be approved by two-thirds of voters instead of a simple majority, and by classifying certain types of taxes — parcel taxes and taxes levied by special districts and school districts — as special taxes subject to higher vote requirements. Extending the two-thirds vote requirement to voter-initiated special tax proposals, as Prop. 43 proposes, would decrease the likelihood that these measures would pass, even if a significant majority of local voters support the measure and the services that the new revenues would fund.
In contrast to the high bar for raising taxes, local governments do not need voter approval to reduce services — and cuts to services often result when localities face revenue shortfalls. Yet, communities also have the option of raising revenues to help close budget gaps. If Prop. 43 passes, counties and cities would still have the ability to raise general taxes with approval from a simple majority of voters to shore up local services. However, local voters’ ability to propose new special taxes to protect or strengthen key services would be limited as local voter initiatives would become much more challenging to pass. Additionally, voters in special districts would face a higher bar to increase revenues to preserve and expand services, regardless of whether the funds would be targeted to specific programs.
Proposition 43’s Constraints on Local Revenues Would Make Things Harder for Communities Already Struggling
Governments across the board have felt the impacts of inflation on the costs of providing public services, and the state’s aging population increasing the cost of providing some services such as health care. The impacts of the 2025 federal budget reconciliation law, (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/hr1-and-the-federal-budget-how-california-leaders-can-respond-to-trumps-cuts/) H.R. 1 — also known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” — along with the effects of climate change, the labor market (https://immresearch.org/reports/ice-arrests-result-in-a-decline-in-employment-state-level-projections/) and broader economic impacts (https://www.bayareaeconomy.org/files/pdf/Economic%20Impact%20of%20Mass%20Deportation_June%202025.pdf) of arrests and deportations of immigrants, and other federal policy changes such as tariffs, are also creating challenges for localities.

I have enough. Let me also quickly read the remainder of the Budget Center brief for the final analysis and see the "supporters and opponents" section, but I think I have plenty.

One more consideration: is there any credible independent analysis arguing the measure is good policy? The Hoover Proposition Lab gives a balanced view; Mercury News endorsed yes ("restore voter-approved restrictions"). SF Chronicle: "we don't support Prop 43 because it further cements a broken system. But ultimately, we won't oppose it, either." LA Times columnist George Skelton: No, because two-thirds requirements are undemocratic.

Weight of considerations:
1. Democratic principle: supermajority requirement for citizen initiatives = minority rule (34% can block 66%). The California Constitution and courts "liberally construe" the initiative power; restricting it is a serious step.
2. Fiscal impact: reduces local revenue during a period of federal cuts (H.R. 1 cuts to Medi-Cal/CalFresh), wildfire costs, housing crisis. Examples: SF Measure C (child care), Fresno Measure P (parks), LA ULA (affordable housing/homelessness), Madera Measure T (transportation) — all passed by majority and would have failed.
3. Renewals/extensions: existing citizen-approved special taxes nearing expiration would need two-thirds to extend — a hidden fiscal cliff.
4. Special districts and school districts: all their taxes are special taxes, so citizen-initiated parcel/special district taxes would need two-thirds, affecting fire districts, hospital districts, transit.
5. Undisclosed provision: subdivision (b) banning citizen-initiated ad valorem property taxes, not mentioned in the AG title/summary or LAO analysis.
6. The official Yes argument contains claims not in the text (spending accountability; "guarantees the right to vote on all local taxes"; transfer-tax protections that were dropped).
7. Provenance: passed as a hostage-negotiation compromise; the author opposes it; legislative leaders and the governor struck a deal to kill a worse measure, but that doesn't make this one good. And its near-unanimous vote is invoked as legitimacy in the Yes rebuttal, which is misleading.
8. Money: Yes side dominated by California Business Roundtable ($11.6M) and real estate interests — motivated by limiting local revenue tools like ULA; the No side is labor/public-service/local-government coalition.

Counterweight for YES: uniform treatment of special taxes regardless of procedural path; prevents well-funded special interests from gaming low-turnout elections; cost-of-living relief. But it cuts no taxes and its practical effect is to make local services harder to fund. Also, the "loophole" framing: the California Supreme Court in Upland itself noted the two-thirds question was left open; lower courts resolved it in favor of majority. The people can decide — but deciding to raise the bar reduces local democratic control.

Given all this, my recommendation: vote NO.

content.thinking:
Very informative. Key additional facts:
- Yes side raised $17.56M, mostly from California Business Roundtable Issues PAC ($11.64M). Against: $9.20M, largest SEIU California State Council $1.5M. So both sides well-funded; the "for" side heavier with corporate money.
- The Yes argument in the voter guide contains claims not supported by the text: "requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved" (not in text — special taxes already must be spent on the specific purpose under existing law: Art XIII C Sec 2(c) "A special tax may not be used for general governmental purposes"), "guarantees voters the right to vote on all local taxes" (already the case), and "protects homeowners from costly new real estate taxes" — but Prop 43 does not cap real estate transfer taxes; that was dropped. Also it mentions transfer taxes as high as 6% — but Prop 43 doesn't change transfer tax rules (they're not ad valorem; they're documentary transfer/excise taxes, still possible via citizen initiative but would require two-thirds as a special tax... wait, would a real estate transfer tax be a "special tax"? Measure ULA was treated as a special tax requiring (under current case law) majority. Under Prop 43 it would need two-thirds. So Prop 43 does make it harder to enact new transfer taxes, but doesn't cap them.)
- The AG title & summary and the LAO analysis do NOT mention subdivision (b) — the flat prohibition on ad valorem property taxes by initiative. That's an undisclosed provision. Actually the AG summary says "This measure would limit voters' ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by raising the percentage..." only. So the property tax ban isn't in the official title and summary. Hmm, that's a notable transparency deficiency.

Let me read the rest of the cityhallpass page (offset 20000) for the interactions with other measures, independent analysis, and polls. Also check the Sacramento Bee editorial and the KQED "why opponents say it would cripple local funding" article. And check the Mercury News endorsement reasoning (YES) to steelman.

Also: interactions — Prop 41 (tax audits: state auditor reviews proposed special taxes before ballot; voids taxes that don't comply with spending limits) and Prop 42 (prohibit new state personal property taxes). These are counter-measures to Prop 40 billionaire tax. Prop 43 fits that cluster: business-funded measures that limit taxation.

Let me fetch more of cityhallpass and the SF Chronicle editorial.

arguments.query: Sacramento Bee editorial "Proposition 43" no 2026 local taxes two-thirds

content.text:
’ rebuttal says “the Legislature’s nearly unanimous vote to place Prop. 43 on the ballot” shows courts “exceeded voters’ intent.” It was signed by Jon Coupal (Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association), Michael Hedges (California Small Business Association) and Greg Van Dyke (California Consumer Advocates for Affordability and Safety) (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, head of Reform California, told the Sacramento Bee editorial board he could find savings “to eliminate the need for a tax increase on any ballot in the state of California this cycle” (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/confused-about-how-to-vote-on-proposition-43-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2csuRb)).
Evolve California argues the measure would make California the hardest state in the country to raise local revenue, the Sacramento Bee reported (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/should-local-taxes-require-two-thirds-voter-approval-proposition-43-explained/ar-AA2crlnQ)).
California YIMBY says the measure would make it harder to raise money for “infrastructure upgrades, affordable housing trust funds, and public transportation,” and would push cities toward higher impact fees on new housing (California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-43-2026/)).
Mott Smith of the Council of Infill Builders, who backed ULA changes, said the industry donors behind the Jarvis initiative “really got absolutely nothing” from the deal (LAist (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure)).
Checking the main claims against official records.
Claim Who makes it What official records show
Restores the two-thirds vote for local special taxes Yes campaign (argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)) The text requires two-thirds for new, increased or extended special taxes, including those proposed by initiative, from Jan. 1, 2027 (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). Taxes already approved are not affected (official summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/title-summary.htm)).
Guarantees voters the right to vote on all local taxes Yes campaign The Constitution already requires voter approval of local general taxes (majority) and special taxes (two-thirds) (Art. XIII C, Sec. 2 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C)). Proposition 43 adds no new election requirement for general taxes (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
Requires governments to spend tax money on the purpose voters approved Yes campaign The text contains no spending rule. It sets vote thresholds and the property-tax limit only (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
Protects homeowners from real estate transfer taxes up to 6% Yes campaign The text does not mention transfer taxes. It would require two-thirds for a new or higher transfer tax only if it is a special tax proposed by voters (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). LA’s ULA rates are 4% and 5.5% (County election results (https://results.lavote.gov/text-results/4300)).
2,000 new or higher local taxes in the past decade Yes campaign We did not find an official count to check this against.
One-third of voters (33.4%) could block a tax No campaign A two-thirds rule means a measure with 66.6% yes fails. The Budget Center gives the example of 35% blocking 65% (California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/)).
The Legislature voted nearly unanimously Yes campaign Senate 35-1 and Assembly 68-2, with 13 members not voting. The author and legislative leaders reached the deal to remove another measure (ACA 22 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22); LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits)).
Makes it harder to fund fire and police No campaign It applies to special taxes proposed by voters. Council-placed special taxes already need two-thirds, and general taxes that can pay for police and fire still need a majority (Art. XIII C, Sec. 2 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C)). The Legislative Analyst says local revenue “could be lower in the future” (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)).
Who supports and opposes it
Supporters
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association of California, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, California Small Business Association and California Consumer Advocates for Affordability and Safety, which signed the guide arguments (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Business Roundtable, through its Issues PAC, the largest donor (Cal-Access, committee 1484860 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484860)).
California Republican Party (CAGOP endorsements (https://cagop.org/endorsements/)).
Reform California and Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/); Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/should-local-taxes-require-two-thirds-voter-approval-proposition-43-explained/ar-AA2crlnQ)).
State Senators Shannon Grove, Tony Strickland and Suzette Valladares, whose ballot measure committees paid for slate mailers supporting it (Cal-Access raw data (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
Opponents
California Professional Firefighters, Nurse Alliance of SEIU California, California School Employees Association, California Federation of Teachers, Californians Against Waste, Communities for a Better Environment, AAPI Force, Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California and Sierra Business Council, as listed in the argument against (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Democratic Party (Inland Valley News (https://inlandvalleynews.com/california-democratic-party-endorses-2026-general-election-candidates-ballot-measures/); KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-43)).
California State Association of Counties and SEIU California (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-43)).
Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, the author (LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits)), and Evolve California (California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/)).
California YIMBY (California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-43-2026/)).
The League of California Cities’ CITIPAC gave $250,000.01 to the No committee (Cal-Access, committee 1492508 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1492508)). A contribution is not the same as a formal endorsement.
Editorial boards.
Yes: the Southern California News Group, in the Daily News and Orange County Register (Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/08/09/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-43-to-make-it-harder-to-raise-taxes/); Orange County Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/09/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-43-to-make-it-harder-to-raise-taxes/)), and the San Diego Union-Tribune (San Diego Union-Tribune (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/04/vote-yes-on-prop-43-to-block-state-supreme-courts-rewrite-of-tax-laws/)). The Mercury News and East Bay Times editorial boards also recommend yes, writing that it “merits support” (Mercury News, Oct. 17, 2026 (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/17/endorsement-back-prop-43-restore-voter-approved-restrictions-on-local-taxes-proposition-13/)).
No: the Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/confused-about-how-to-vote-on-proposition-43-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2csuRb)).
Neither: the San Francisco Chronicle editorial board wrote, “We don’t support Prop 43 because it further cements a broken system. But ultimately, we won’t oppose it, either” (San Francisco Chronicle, Oct. 23, 2026 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-43-ballot-california-22477053.php)).
We found no LA Times editorial board position as of Sept. 30, 2026.
Money for and against
For Proposition 43 Against Proposition 43
Committees Two: Yes on Prop 43 - The Local Taxpayer Protection Act (ID 1484860) and Yes on Prop. 43, a Project of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (ID 1493012) One: No on Prop 43: Stop the Local Taxpayer Deception Act, sponsored by labor organizations (ID 1492508)
Raised, Jan. 1, 2025 to Oct. 17, 2026 $15,417,784.02 $7,742,284.74
Spent, same period $15,567,031.80 $6,622,177.15
Cash on hand, Oct. 17, 2026 $244,784.93 $1,152,357.59
Late contributions reported Oct. 18 to Nov. 1 $2,141,383.93 $1,459,000
Source: the committees’ campaign statements for committee 1484860 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484860), committee 1493012 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1493012) and committee 1492508 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1492508), read from the Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip) dated Nov. 2, 2026, and added up by CityHallPass. The latest statements cover Sept. 20 to Oct. 17 (1484860 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3215138&amendid=0); 1493012 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3214623&amendid=0); 1492508 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3215820&amendid=0)). The No committee reported $32,250 in unpaid bills on Oct. 17. Interactions with other measures on this ballot
City Measure FD. Decided under the majority rule, as described above . California Professional Firefighters signed the argument against Proposition 43 and supports FD (Prop. 43 arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm); our Measure FD page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/measure-fd)).
Propositions 40, 41 and 42. These deal with state taxes. The Legislative Analyst flags possible conflicts among 40, 41 and 42, but not with Proposition 43 (Legislative Analyst, Proposition 41 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/analysis.htm)). See our Proposition 41 (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-41) and Proposition 42 (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/prop-42) pages.
If it passes
When it starts. A constitutional amendment takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote, and it may set a later operative date (State Constitution, Art. XVIII, Sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)). The new two-thirds rule begins Jan. 1, 2027 (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
What it covers. New, increased or extended special taxes proposed by voters and approved after Jan. 1, 2027 (official summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/title-summary.htm); Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)).
Open questions. Subdivision (b), on taxes based on property value, is not explained in the Legislative Analyst’s analysis (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)). Burke, Williams & Sorensen says it will watch “any subsequent litigation or implementing legislation” (California City News (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)). We found no lawsuit filed against the measure as of Sept. 30, 2026.
Key moments
We found no televised debate on Proposition 43 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
Deal and same-day vote (June 25, 2026). The Jarvis initiative and ACA 13 were pulled and ACA 22 passed both houses the same day (ACA 22 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22); LAist (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure); Burke, Williams & Sorensen (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)).
